source.notes: Depreciation and amortisation as a share of capital expenditure, at the FY2019 actual = 1.4990 (2,154 $mm of D&A over 1,437 $mm of capex). Both terms come from the same cash flow statement, recorded at tools/data_fabric/out/TSLA_alphavantage_cash_flow.json; taking them from different sources would make the ratio meaningless, because the two sources scope capex differently. Together with row 10 this reproduces the observed FY2019 D&A of 0.0876 of revenue exactly, since 0.058467 x 1.498956 = 0.087639. CAVEAT, and it matters: this ratio is unstable across the window (0.40, 0.82, 1.50), because Tesla's capex fell by two thirds while its asset base kept depreciating. The pairing is chosen so that the product ties to the one quantity that is stable -- D&A as a share of revenue, which ran 0.1391, 0.0886 and 0.0876 across the window. Read row 9 and row 10 as a pair, not separately.

source.notes: Capital expenditure over revenue held at the FY2019 actual, 1,437 / 24,578 = 0.0585, from the cash flow statement recorded at tools/data_fabric/out/TSLA_alphavantage_cash_flow.json. source.notes: Real disclosed primary share issuance.

source.name: Tesla's February 2020 raise was a single underwritten primary offering -- no separate rights offering occurred, so no shares were issued through a rights mechanism
source.notes: Left at the template default of 25 (placeholder rights-shares-issued) before this fix. The 'Rights Offering' sheet's own C6 ('Rights shares offered') reads 'Cap Table & Dilution'!C8, not C7 -- so despite C7 already correctly holding the real 2.65mm primary share count, the Rights Offering sheet's downstream computation (C16-C19) was pulling 25mm phantom rights shares, producing an 'Expected net rights proceeds' of ~$19.175bn on the Decision & Checks dashboard (row 23) for a transaction that raised about $2bn total. Setting this to 0 correctly reflects that no rights offering happened, without touching the already-correct C7/C11-driven primary-offering figures (Cap Table 'Gross/Net primary proceeds', matching the case's recorded forecast/realized).

source.notes: Depreciation, amortisation and impairment for FY2017 = 1,636 $mm, from Tesla's cash flow statement as recorded at tools/data_fabric/out/TSLA_alphavantage_cash_flow.json. WHY NOT EDGAR: Tesla tagged DepreciationDepletionAndAmortization in one filing only, with a narrower figure (769 $mm for FY2017 against 1,636 $mm here), and did not tag it at all for FY2018 or FY2019. refresh.trigger: Historical actuals block filled after the BASE template fix
refresh.what_changed: The BASE template's income-statement historical block carried no input marker and no derived formulas, so the income statement, the DCF, and diluted EPS all evaluated to zero. With the template fixed, this fills FY2017-FY2019 revenue, cost of revenue, operating expense, depreciation and amortisation, interest, tax, and share count. Depreciation comes from the cash flow statement rather than EDGAR, because Tesla tagged EDGAR's D&A concept in one filing only and with a narrower figure. With D&A real and taken out of the operating expense row, the EBITDA line is a real EBITDA and EBIT ties exactly to the disclosed operating income in all three years.
refresh.reviewer_notes: External historical case; human stakeholder approval remains pending. Read three things before using any number here. First, the share counts are period-end outstanding rather than weighted diluted, which understates earnings per share. Second, the forward D&A driver is the product of a capex ratio and a D&A-to-capex ratio, and the second of those is unstable across the window; the pair is set so the product ties to D&A as a share of revenue, which is stable, and the two rows must be read together. Third, the discounted cash flow values the equity at roughly a quarter of the price the February 2020 offering actually cleared at. That is not a defect in the arithmetic. It is what a cash flow model built on Tesla's FY2019 operating margins produces, and the gap between the two was the whole argument about Tesla at the time. The case exists to show the offering mechanics, not to settle that argument.
